title: Decision surface and arena: what would the model do here?
summary: A colour map of a classifier's probability over feature space, the decision boundary at one half, the training data on top and a cursor that reports the model's answer at one point. It shows the model's behaviour everywhere, not just on the data.

media.alt: A colour map of class probability over a two-dimensional feature plane with an amber decision boundary, circles and triangles for two classes and a cursor with a boxed probability readout.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What would the model do here?
read_the_figure.axes: x: feature 1, y: feature 2 (both dimensionless, -3 to 3). Colour: P(class 1) from 0 (purple) to 1 (yellow). Amber curve: decision boundary at P = 0.5. White circles: class 0 data; triangles: class 1 data. Rose cursor at (0.5, -0.6) with a box: model says P = 0.55.
look_at: Where does the amber boundary run, and how smooth is it?
Are the data on the right sides? Count the exceptions near the boundary.
How wide is the region of intermediate colours (uncertain)?
What does the model do where there is no data (corners)?
read_the_figure.proves: It shows what the model does at every point of the plane, including where it has no data, and how the data fall relative to its boundary. It does not show whether the model is right where there is no data, and nothing of real-world cost.
if_wrong: Data not overlaid: the surface cannot be judged against anything.
A confident colour far from all data: extrapolation presented as knowledge.
Colour scale without units or a stated meaning: P(class 1) must be said.

terms.meaning: The set of points where the model's output crosses the threshold (here P = 0.5).
The model's predicted probability of class 1 at every point of the feature plane.
The S-shaped function that turns a score z into a probability: P = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)).
An interactive view in which the reader places a cursor and sees the model's response.
Predicting where there is no training data.

remember: Colour gives P, the amber line is P = 0.5.
Always overlay the data and use different shapes for classes.
Confident away from the data means the model is extrapolating.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position in the plane encodes the two features; colour encodes P(class 1) with a perceptual map from purple to yellow; the amber contour at P = 0.5 is the boundary. Circles and triangles (shape, not just colour) encode the true class. The rose cross and circle mark the cursor, with a boxed callout stating the model's answer there.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A classifier is a function on feature space, and the most direct way to understand a function on a plane is to draw it. The boundary is the one line that matters for decisions, and the colour gradient shows how fast confidence changes across it. Overlaying the data shows how well the model matches reality, and the cursor lets the reader query it at one chosen point.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What does the model say at the cursor? P = 0.55: the cursor at (0.5, -0.6) is almost on the amber boundary, so the model is nearly undecided. Q2: How many points lie on the wrong side? A few near the boundary: for example the white circle at about (0.95, -0.97) lies on the yellow side, so it is a class-0 point predicted as class 1, and two or three triangles sit close to the line; the great majority are clearly right. Q3: What happens in the corners? The top right is saturated yellow and the bottom left saturated purple, with no data beyond about 2.5: the model is extrapolating with full confidence there.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Data overlaid: the points are the only evidence the surface is any good. A probability map without the data is a picture of the model, not a test of it.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A colour map can look confident where the model knows nothing: at the corners the colour saturates to purple or yellow although there is no data. The boundary is drawn at P = 0.5, which is a choice, not necessarily the best for the use. A two-feature plane hides everything the other features do. The map is a property of the model, not the world: a smooth surface may still be wrong. Static previews cannot show the response as the cursor moves. The training points are shown but not validation points.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A confusion matrix and ROC curve summarise performance without a picture. Calibration plots check that P means what it says. Partial dependence for models with more features. An uncertainty map (standard deviation of an ensemble) next to the probability map.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second panel with the ensemble spread, shade the region with no data within a distance 1, and mark the points of a validation set with a different marker.

worked.title: Reading the cursor
worked.problem: At the cursor (0.5, -0.6) the model's score is z = 0.8 - 0.84 + 0.3 sin(1) = 0.21. Find P, and the distance in odds from the boundary.
worked.answer: P = 0.55, odds 1.24 to 1: the model is almost indifferent, very close to the boundary.

checks.q: What does the amber line mark?
The model is confident (P = 0.99) at (-3, -3), outside the data. What do you tell the user?
checks.answer: The model has seen no data there; its confidence comes from the shape of the function, not evidence, so treat the prediction as unsupported.
